title: Lobos to Buenos Aires — the Journey of the Conductor and the Descamisados
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Pampa and the Patagonian Boyhood

stops.name: Lobos — the adobe rancho on the pampa
stops.campa: On the eighth of October a boy is born in a low adobe rancho at Lobos, on the flat green immensity of the Buenos Aires pampa — natural son of Mario Tomás Perón and the criolla Juana Sosa. The gauchos come and go across the plain; the horizon is one unbroken line. He is baptized Juan Domingo. Later chroniclers will dispute the year and the place, whispering 1893, whispering Roque Pérez — but the register at Lobos names the day, and the day is kept. From this humble ground the man who will move millions is lifted into the world.
stops.quote: Nací en un hogar de clase media, mi padre era criador de ovejas.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, autobiographical recollections ('Del poder al exilio')
suggested_refs: The casa natal de Perón museum at Lobos

stops.name: Río Gallegos — the estancias of the far south
stops.campa: The family embarks on the ship Santa Cruz for the ends of the earth. Mario Tomás, restless, seeks fortune in sheep on the wind-scoured estancias near Río Gallegos — Chaok-Aike, Kamesa-Aike, Coy-Aike, names the Tehuelche gave the land. The five-year-old learns cold that cuts and a sky that never ends. Here the pampa's boy becomes a child of Patagonia, riding before he can well walk, watching the shearers and the peones. The frontier teaches him the first lesson of his life: that the men who do the labor are the men who hold the country up.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the Perón family's Santa Cruz estancias
The Tehuelche place-names of the estancias

stops.name: Camarones — the port town and the justice of the peace
stops.campa: In February the family moves north to Camarones, a huddle of houses on the Chubut coast where the sea batters a rocky bay. Mario Tomás serves as juez de paz, dispensing rough justice among the settlers and the natives; the boy watches his father weigh disputes and knows the shape of authority up close. He roams the meseta on horseback, learns to shoot, learns the silence of great distances. Later, when he is master of a nation, Perón will say the Patagonian frontier made him — that there a man was measured only by what he could do.
suggested_refs: The Perón family house at Camarones (Museo de la Familia Perón)
Camarones bay and the Chubut meseta

stops.name: Sierra Cuadrada — the estancia La Porteña
stops.campa: The family gains its own land at last: La Porteña, a stone-and-adobe house in the Sierra Cuadrada, inland from Comodoro Rivadavia. Wind, sheep, and the great arid plateau. Every summer of his boyhood the boy returns here from the schools of the capital, and the bond with this land never breaks — decades later, as president, he will nearly move here with Evita. The Patagonian summers forge in him the endurance of a mountain man and a deep, wordless conviction that the interior, the forgotten south, is the true heart of the country.
suggested_refs: La Porteña — the chalet de piedra in Sierra Cuadrada

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the Colegio Militar de la Nación
stops.campa: On the first of March the tall, athletic boy from Patagonia enters the Colegio Militar de la Nación, a scholarship won for him carrying him past the gate. He is a natural: fencer, boxer, gymnast, a rider already hardened by the south. Discipline, hierarchy, the science of command — these become his native tongue. On the thirteenth of December 1913 he graduates subteniente of infantry, forty-third of sixty-four in the 38th promotion. The army will be his home, his school, and his instrument for four decades; the boy of the estancias has become an officer of the Republic.
suggested_refs: Cadet portrait of Perón at the Colegio Militar
Colegio Militar de la Nación, El Palomar

stops.name: Paraná — the young lieutenant of the 12th Infantry
stops.campa: The new subteniente takes his first post with the 12th Infantry Regiment at Paraná on the river. He drills conscripts drawn from the poorest of the provinces, and among these barefoot boys of the interior he learns something the salons of Buenos Aires never taught: how the humble Argentine lives, what he suffers, what he is owed. The officer discovers a talent for winning men — for being loved by those beneath him without loss of command. It is the seed of everything: the conductor of masses is first the captain who is followed gladly.

stops.name: Campo de Mayo — instructor at the School of Non-Commissioned Officers
stops.campa: At the vast garrison of Campo de Mayo Perón serves as instructor at the Escuela de Suboficiales through the early twenties, teaching the sergeants who are the true spine of the army. He writes manuals; he masters the art of explaining, of making the complex simple, of speaking so that a plain man understands and obeys with pride. The suboficiales are drawn from the people, and they will remember him. When the crisis comes in 1945, it is this bond — the officer beloved of the ranks — that helps carry him from prison to the balcony.
suggested_refs: Escuela de Suboficiales, Campo de Mayo

stops.name: Buenos Aires — professor at the Escuela Superior de Guerra
stops.campa: Captain, then major, Perón teaches military history at the Escuela Superior de Guerra, the War College, through the thirties. He studies the great captains — the Napoleonic wars, the strategy of concentration, the theory of the offensive — and he writes on Argentine military history and on the frontier campaigns. In these years the tactician becomes a thinker of national organization, brooding on the state, on discipline, on the mobilization of a whole people. The professor of strategy is quietly assembling the doctrine that will one day be called Justicialismo.
suggested_refs: Escuela Superior de Guerra, Buenos Aires

segments.name: The Italian Years — the Mountain and the Corporazione

stops.name: Rome — arrival of the military observer
stops.campa: In February Perón arrives in Rome as military observer to Mussolini's Italy, sent to study the alpine troops and the new corporate state. He is forty-three, a lieutenant colonel, keen-eyed and hungry to learn. He walks the imperial capital under its fascist banners and studies how a whole nation is being organized — labor, capital, and state braided into a single corporate body. What he sees will haunt his own doctrine: the Third Position, neither capitalist nor communist, the organized community. But he comes above all as a soldier of the mountains, and to the mountains he goes.

stops.name: Merano — the Tridentina Alpine Division
stops.campa: In July Perón joins the Alpine Division Tridentina at Merano and Bolzano in the Dolomites — the very valleys through which, a century and a half before, Goethe crossed toward Italy. Here the Argentine officer trains with the Alpini, the elite mountain infantry, on rock and ice and glacier. He climbs, he skis, he lives among the crack troops of the Alps and earns their respect. The endurance of the Patagonian boyhood serves him now; the man who rode the Sierra Cuadrada takes to the high peaks as if born to them.

stops.name: Aosta — the Alpine School and the roof of the Alps
stops.campa: At the Scuola di Alpinismo of Aosta, beneath the giants of Mont Blanc and the Gran Paradiso, Perón completes his training as a mountain officer and is decorated by his superiors as a distinguished alpino. He also attaches to the Pinerolo division in Piedmont. These are the finest professional months of his soldiering: to master the highest and hardest ground, among the best troops of a European army. He will carry the Cóndor de los Andes, the mountain-troop badge, and the memory of these peaks all his life.

stops.name: Rome — Piazza Venezia, the day of the declaration of war
stops.campa: On the tenth of June Perón stands in the Piazza Venezia among the roaring crowd as Mussolini appears on the balcony and hurls Italy into the war. The Argentine watches the theatre of the balcony, the ocean of upturned faces, the single voice commanding the multitude — and something is fixed in him forever. He has seen how a leader and a people become one body across a square. Five years and four months later, from a balcony over the Plaza de Mayo, he will answer that vision with one of his own, and the descamisados will roar back.
suggested_refs: Newsreel of the 10 June 1940 declaration of war

segments.name: The Revolution, the Workers, and the Seventeenth of October

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the GOU and the coup of 1943
stops.campa: On the fourth of June the army marches on the Casa Rosada and sweeps away the corrupt conservative order. Colonel Perón is a founder and hidden engine of the GOU, the Grupo de Oficiales Unidos, the lodge of nationalist officers behind the rising. He takes no throne; he takes the small, despised office of labor. Others reach for war ministries and provinces. Perón, alone among them, sees that power in the twentieth century lies not in the barracks but in the workshops — in the millions of workers no one has ever asked to speak.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the Secretaría de Trabajo y Previsión
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of November the old Department of Labor is raised into a Secretaría de Trabajo y Previsión, and Perón takes command. From this desk he changes everything: the eight-hour day, paid holidays, the aguinaldo, pensions, labor courts, the statute of the peón. The unions, long ignored and repressed, find in this colonel a patron who signs their demands into law. Worker by worker, contract by contract, he wins the whole laboring class to himself. He will call this the true beginning of his movement — the initial day.
stops.quote: El día que creamos la Secretaría de Trabajo y Previsión, para mí es el día inicial de nuestro movimiento.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, on the founding of the Secretaría de Trabajo y Previsión
suggested_refs: The Secretaría de Trabajo building, Buenos Aires

stops.name: San Juan — the earthquake and the festival of the ruins
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of January the earth heaves and San Juan falls to rubble; ten thousand die beneath their houses. Perón, from Trabajo y Previsión, throws the state into the rescue and the relief, and calls the nation to give. He summons artists and public to a great solidarity festival at Luna Park in Buenos Aires. Out of catastrophe he forges a mystique of the caring state — and out of the festival's crowd, on the twenty-second, a young radio actress will step into his life and change the history of the country.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Luna Park, the meeting with Eva Duarte
stops.campa: On the night of the twenty-second, at the San Juan relief festival in Luna Park, the widower colonel is seated beside a slender radio actress of twenty-four, María Eva Duarte, natural daughter of the provinces, who has climbed from nothing by will alone. They speak, and by the small hours of the twenty-third they are not to part again. She becomes his companion, his voice among the poor and the women, his fiercest instrument. Two ambitions of the humble, meeting; from this night the myth of Perón and Evita is born.
stops.quote_source: Words attributed to Eva Duarte at the Luna Park meeting (Peronist tradition)
suggested_refs: Early photographs of Perón and Eva Duarte, 1944

stops.name: Isla Martín García — the prisoner in the river
stops.campa: His rivals in the army, terrified of the labor colonel's power, force his resignation and on the thirteenth of October seize him and carry him to the island prison of Martín García in the estuary. There he sits, the whole edifice of his rise apparently thrown down in a week. He writes to Eva; he feigns illness, and a sympathetic doctor certifies a pleurisy, the pretext to bring him back to the continent and the Hospital Militar. In the workshops and the tanneries of the industrial belt, meanwhile, a fury is rising that no barracks can imagine.
suggested_refs: Perón's letters from Martín García to Eva

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo — the balcony and the descamisados, 17 October 1945
stops.campa: From dawn on the seventeenth the workers pour out of the industrial suburbs and across the bridges into the Plaza de Mayo — in shirtsleeves, sleeves rolled, the descamisados, the shirtless ones, cooling their feet in the fountains under the winter-spring sun. They will not leave until Perón is free. All day the multitude swells and roars his name. At last, near eleven at night, he steps onto the balcony of the Casa Rosada, and a nation of the humble roars back. The people have taken him from prison and set him on the balcony. Peronism is born this day.
stops.quote: Hace casi dos años, desde estos mismos balcones, dije que tenía tres honras en mi vida: la de ser soldado, la de ser un patriota y la de ser el primer trabajador argentino.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, speech from the balcony of the Casa Rosada, 17 October 1945
suggested_refs: Photograph of the descamisados with feet in the Plaza de Mayo fountains
Audio recording of the 17 October 1945 balcony speech

stops.name: Junín — the marriage to Eva
stops.campa: Five days after the balcony, on the twenty-second, Perón and Eva marry at the civil registry in Junín, her home town, Domingo Mercante and her brother Juan Duarte as witnesses. The colonel raised back to power by the people takes as wife the woman who will become their saint. The private bond is sealed just as the public triumph crests. Together now, publicly and lawfully, they turn to the campaign that will make him president — she at his side on every whistle-stop, her voice reaching where his cannot.
suggested_refs: Wedding photograph of Perón and Eva, 1945

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the inauguration, first presidency
stops.campa: Having won the February election against the whole array of the oligarchy and the American ambassador, on the fourth of June Perón takes the presidential sash and the baton in the Casa Rosada. The descamisados fill the plaza again, this time in triumph. He proclaims a new Argentina founded on three banners — political sovereignty, economic independence, social justice — and a Third Position between the empires of capital and communism. The labor colonel is now the constitutional president, and the doctrine of Justicialismo becomes the law of a state.

stops.name: Tucumán — the Declaration of Economic Independence and the First Five-Year Plan
stops.campa: On the ninth of July, anniversary of independence, at the historic house of Tucumán where the fathers once broke from Spain, Perón signs a second declaration — of economic independence — and unveils the First Five-Year Plan. The state will industrialize the country, build steel and power at San Nicolás and in Jujuy, throw off the tutelage of foreign capital. He binds the new economic sovereignty to the old political one, standing on the very ground of 1816. Argentina, he declares, will belong to Argentines and above all to those who work her.
stops.quote: Soberanía política, independencia económica y justicia social.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, the three banners proclaimed with the First Five-Year Plan, Tucumán, 1947
suggested_refs: Casa Histórica de la Independencia, Tucumán

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the female vote and the rise of Evita
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of September the law is proclaimed: the women of Argentina shall vote. Eva stands at the heart of it, and from the balcony she shows the enacted law to the crowd of women below. She has become a power in her own right — patron of the poor through her Foundation, voice of the shirtless, terror of the oligarchy — building a fervor that will make her, in the eyes of millions, a saint. The Peronist movement now stands on two legs: the conductor Perón and the abanderada Evita.
stops.quote: Mujeres de mi Patria, recibo en este instante, de manos del Gobierno de la Nación, la ley que consagra nuestros derechos cívicos.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, on the proclamation of women's suffrage, 23 September 1947
suggested_refs: Eva Perón showing the suffrage law from the balcony

stops.name: Retiro — the nationalization of the railways
stops.campa: On the first of March the British-owned railways pass into Argentine hands, and the state takes formal possession at Retiro. A vast crowd of descamisados fills the plaza before the great terminus; banners read Los ferrocarriles son argentinos — the railways are Argentine. The steel arteries that carried Argentine wealth to the ports for foreign profit are national now. It is the highest emblem of economic independence, the Five-Year Plan made iron and rail, and the crowd celebrates it as a second liberation from empire.
stops.quote_source: Peronist proclamation on the nationalization of the railways, 1 March 1948
suggested_refs: Retiro station and the 1948 nationalization rally

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Eva's renunciamiento
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of August a vast open-air Cabildo of the people fills Avenida 9 de Julio, demanding that Eva stand as vice-president beside Perón. She is dying of cancer, though few yet know it, and the army will not have her. Wracked and beloved, she begs the multitude for time, then renounces the honor. Her renunciamiento is a passion play performed before the nation; the poor weep in the streets. She has refused the crown and thereby become greater than any office — the martyr of the descamisados.
stops.quote: Yo no renuncio a la lucha ni al trabajo... renuncio a los honores.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, the renunciamiento speech, 22 August 1951
suggested_refs: Cabildo Abierto del Justicialismo, 9 de Julio

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the death of Evita
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of July, at eight twenty-five in the evening, Eva dies in the presidential residence, thirty-three years old, worn to nothing by the cancer. The radio breaks the news to a stunned country: the Spiritual Leader of the Nation has passed into immortality. The nation halts; the poor line the streets for a fortnight of mourning, the flowers of Buenos Aires exhausted before the grief. Perón has lost the abanderada of his movement. Her embalmed body, meant for a great monument never built, is about to begin an odyssey stranger than any in his own long journey.
stops.quote: Eva Perón entró en la inmortalidad.
stops.quote_source: National radio announcement of Eva Perón's death, 26 July 1952
suggested_refs: Eva Perón lying in state, CGT building
The embalmed body of Eva Perón

segments.name: The Bombing, the Fall, and the Long Exile

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo — the bombing of the Plaza
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of June the navy and rebel air force turn on the capital itself: aircraft cross the sky over Buenos Aires and drop more than a hundred bombs, nine to fourteen tons of explosive, onto the Plaza de Mayo to kill the president and his cabinet. They miss Perón but slaughter the people — some three hundred dead, near a thousand wounded, most of them civilians crossing the square, a trolley of workers among the bodies. It is a massacre without precedent in the city's history, and the prelude, in three months, to his fall.
suggested_refs: Monument to the victims of the 1955 Plaza de Mayo bombing
Photographs of the bombed Plaza de Mayo

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the Revolución Libertadora and the fall
stops.campa: In September the self-styled Revolución Libertadora rises across the country, and by the nineteenth Perón resigns rather than plunge Argentina into civil war. Ten years to the month since the descamisados carried him to the balcony, the conductor is thrown down. He seeks asylum in the Paraguayan embassy and takes refuge aboard the Paraguayan gunboat in the river. The victors will ban his very name; to say 'Perón' becomes a crime. Thus begins an exile that will last eighteen years — and a resistance that will not die.

stops.name: Asunción and Villarrica — the first refuge
stops.campa: A Paraguayan flying-boat carries the fallen president across the border in early October, and he is sheltered first in Asunción and then, from the seventeenth — the sacred date of his movement — in the country estate of a Colorado leader at Villarrica among the orange groves. The people of Paraguay throng to glimpse him; the exile is already a legend. But Argentine pressure closes in, and in early November a plane lifts him away toward Central America. The odyssey of the exiled conductor, like San Martín's and O'Higgins's before him, is truly begun.

stops.name: Colón, Panama — the exile and the meeting with Isabel
stops.campa: In Panama the exile lives modestly — the Hotel Washington in Colón, then a small chalet lent by the town. And here, in the cabaret Happyland, he meets a dancer of twenty-four, María Estela Martínez, called Isabel, touring with a ballet company. He buys out her contract for three hundred dollars, and by late January she is his companion. As Eva rose from the radio, Isabel rises from the cabaret; the widower takes to his side the woman who will one day, incredibly, succeed him as president of Argentina.
suggested_refs: The Happyland cabaret and Isabel Martínez

stops.name: Caracas — exile under the Venezuelan sun
stops.campa: From Panama, by way of Nicaragua and Maracaibo, Perón reaches Caracas in August and settles in the Venezuela of Pérez Jiménez. From here he directs the first threads of the Peronist Resistance at home, where his followers strike and sabotage and scrawl his forbidden name on every wall. He nearly perishes in a bomb attack on his residence. When Pérez Jiménez is overthrown in January 1958 the ground shifts under him again, and he must move on — to the last and strangest of his Caribbean stations.

stops.name: Ciudad Trujillo — the court of the dictator
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of January Perón lands in the Dominican Republic, in the capital that the tyrant Trujillo has named after himself. He lodges at the Jaragua, then, for economy, the Hotel Paz. For two years he lives under the shadow of the most absolute despot of the Caribbean, plotting his return by letter and messenger. When even this refuge sours, on the twenty-sixth of January 1960 he boards a plane once more — this time for Spain, and the villa at Puerta de Hierro where the long heart of the exile awaits.

segments.name: Madrid — the Villa, the Corpse, and the Return

stops.name: Madrid — the villa at Puerta de Hierro
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of January Perón reaches Franco's Spain and settles at last in a quinta near Puerta de Hierro on the edge of Madrid — the house they call 17 de Octubre. Here he will spend twelve of his eighteen exiled years and govern Argentina from afar. Pilgrims of Peronism cross the ocean to kiss his hand; he receives union bosses and young guerrillas alike, dispensing tapes, letters, and cryptic blessings to every faction. From this suburban villa, by messenger and magnetic tape, the banned old conductor rules a country that will not let him go.
suggested_refs: The Puerta de Hierro villa '17 de Octubre'
Perón's audio tapes sent to Argentina

stops.name: Milan — the hidden corpse of Eva
stops.campa: While Perón wanders his exile, the body of Eva undergoes an odyssey of its own. The Revolución Libertadora, fearing the dead saint more than the living leader, steals the embalmed corpse and hides it, at last burying it in secret under a false name — María Maggi de Magistris — in the Musocco cemetery of Milan. For sixteen years the incorruptible Evita lies concealed in Italian soil while the man who loved her governs from Madrid. Only in 1971 will the generals confess the grave and return her to him.
suggested_refs: The false grave of 'María Maggi de Magistris'

stops.name: Puerta de Hierro — Eva restored
stops.campa: On the third of September the coffin comes home to Puerta de Hierro. After sixteen years lost, the body of Eva is returned to Perón in Madrid, still uncannily preserved. In the villa it is kept, and the tale runs that José López Rega, the dark occultist counselor now shadowing the household, performs his rites over the corpse — seeking to pass Eva's power into Isabel, the third wife. The saint of the descamisados lies again beside the conductor, on the eve of his impossible return, wrapped now in rumor and in cult.
suggested_refs: Eva's coffin returned to Puerta de Hierro, 1971
José López Rega and the villa

stops.name: Ezeiza — the first return, 17 November 1972
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of November, after seventeen years of banishment, Perón lands at Ezeiza on Argentine soil — an old man of seventy-seven stepping off the plane into a downpour and a sea of the faithful, held back by the still-frightened generals. He stays only weeks, but the spell is broken: the exile has touched the homeland and lived. He anoints Héctor Cámpora to run in his place, and Cámpora wins. The road is open now for the definitive return — and for the tragedy that will stain it.
suggested_refs: Perón descending at Ezeiza in the rain, 1972

stops.name: Ezeiza — the return and the massacre, 20 June 1973
stops.campa: On the twentieth of June Perón returns for good, and the greatest crowd in Argentine history — some two million — floods the highways to Ezeiza to receive him. But at the speakers' platform, right-wing Peronists open fire on the leftist columns of the Montoneros and the FAR as they approach: thirteen dead, hundreds wounded, the woods of Ezeiza turned to a killing ground. The old man's plane is diverted; the day of homecoming becomes a massacre. The two faces of his movement, the union right and the guerrilla left, have drawn each other's blood at the very hour of his triumph.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the third presidency
stops.campa: In September the people return him to power with sixty-two percent of the vote, his third wife Isabel as vice-president, and on the twelfth of October Perón takes the sash for the third time — twenty-seven years after the first. He is old and mortally ill, come home to a country tearing itself apart between the factions of his own name. He labors to calm the violence, to hold the center, to bind up the movement. But the guerrillas he once blessed he now casts out, and the old conductor's last months are a struggle to master the storm he himself has raised.
stops.quote: Nunca me he sentido otra cosa que un hombre demasiado humilde al servicio de una causa siempre demasiado grande para mí.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, speech to Congress on his return, 21 June 1973
suggested_refs: Perón and Isabel take office, October 1973

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo — the last balcony, 'the most marvelous music'
stops.campa: On the twelfth of June, gravely ill, Perón comes onto the balcony of the Casa Rosada one last time and speaks to a filled Plaza de Mayo — the same square where the descamisados carried him up in 1945. Thirteen minutes only, and it sounds like a farewell. He tells the multitude he carries in his ears the most marvelous music of all, the voice of the Argentine people. Nineteen days later he will be dead. The circle of his journey closes on the balcony where it turned, the leader and the plaza speaking to each other for the last time.
stops.quote: Llevo en mis oídos la más maravillosa música que, para mí, es la palabra del pueblo argentino.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, final speech from the Casa Rosada balcony, 12 June 1974
suggested_refs: Recording of the 'más maravillosa música' speech

stops.name: Olivos — the death of the Conductor
stops.campa: On the first of July, at a quarter past one in the afternoon, Juan Domingo Perón dies of heart failure in the presidential quinta at Olivos, seventy-eight years old. Isabel, his widow and vice-president, announces to the nation in a broken voice the passing of the apostle of peace, and succeeds him — the first woman to hold the presidency of Argentina. A whole country weeps in the winter rain and files past the coffin. The boy of the Lobos rancho, master of his people to the end, has finished his journey; but the movement, and the strife, will outlive him.
stops.quote: Ha muerto el apóstol de la paz.
stops.quote_source: María Estela Martínez de Perón, national announcement of Perón's death, 1 July 1974
suggested_refs: Perón lying in state, Congreso, July 1974
